title: Importing Nonverbal Deception Cues to LLM Token-Level Analysis
original_idea: Analyze token probability distributions in LLM outputs under honest vs. deceptive conditions. Test whether specific token-level signals differ systematically between conditions. Use a model where deceptive conditions are experimentally controlled.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: involuntary token-level signals during deception -> lightweight detection mechanism. The analogy to human nonverbal cues is interesting but the link is speculative -- there is no reason to assume LLM generation processes produce involuntary signals analogous to biological involuntary responses.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Token probability analysis via APIs is technically accessible. The experimental setup (comparing honest vs deceptive conditions) requires a controlled deception setup but could leverage existing datasets. Statistical analysis of probability distributions is intermediate-level work.

narrow_scope.reasoning: A first deliverable exists (statistical comparison of token probability distributions in honest vs deceptive conditions), but requires setting up controlled deception conditions and defining which token-level features to measure. Moderate effort to first result.

novelty.reasoning: Token-level and activation-level analysis of deception in LLMs is an active area. Research using contrastive activations shows honest vs. deceptive representations separate into distinct clusters around layer 8. The 'Obfuscation Atlas' (arXiv:2602.15515, 2026) maps where honesty emerges using deception probes. Apollo Research's linear probes on residual-stream activations achieve F1 up to 95% for deception detection. DeceptionBench (arXiv:2510.15501) provides 150 scenarios for evaluating deceptive tendencies. The specific framing of 'nonverbal cue analogues' at the token probability level is somewhat novel, but the underlying methodology (comparing probability distributions in honest vs. deceptive conditions) is substantially covered by existing white-box deception detection work. The gap is the specific analogy-driven feature selection inspired by human nonverbal cues.
